These are estimates from tape measurements, not a clinical body-composition assessment. Trends over time are more meaningful than any single number.
Everything that isn\'t fat — muscle, bone, organs and water. A tape measure can\'t separate muscle from the rest, so this is the closest honest figure.
Your weight multiplied by body-fat percentage.
Lean mass scaled to your height, so it compares fairly across body sizes. This is the usual stand-in for "how muscular am I". Around 25 (men) or 19 (women) is near the drug-free ceiling.
Waist divided by height. Predicts metabolic risk better than BMI because it reflects fat around the organs. The rule of thumb: keep your waist under half your height.
Waist divided by hips, using WHO thresholds. Reflects where fat is stored — around the middle carries more risk than around the hips.
The weight span matching BMI 18.5–24.9 at your height. BMI ignores build and muscle, so treat this as a rough guide.

Ratios between your circumferences. Unlike the risk metrics above, there is no medical threshold for these — the commonly quoted "ideal" figures are aesthetic conventions, not health targets. They are most useful watched over time: a rising chest-to-waist means the waist held while the chest grew.

A large Danish cohort study linked thigh circumference under about 60 cm to higher cardiovascular risk, independent of body fat — muscle in the legs appears protective. It is one study on one population, so read it as context, not a verdict.
Each measurement against your previous entry and your first one. Whether a number should go up or down depends on your goal, so no direction is marked good or bad here.

Stand relaxed with your head facing forward. Wrap the tape around the neck just below the larynx (Adam\'s apple), perpendicular to the long axis of the neck. Keep the tape level — not slanting downward at the front. Read at the end of a normal exhale.

Stand relaxed and breathe out. Wrap the tape around the natural waist — the narrowest point of the torso, typically about 2.5 cm (1 in) above the navel. Keep the tape parallel to the floor and snug, but not compressing the skin.
Stand with feet together. Wrap the tape around the widest part of your buttocks/hips — check sideways in a mirror to find it. Keep the tape level all the way around and snug, not tight.

Stand relaxed with arms at your sides. Wrap the tape around the fullest part of your chest — across the nipple line for men, across the bust for women. Keep it level all the way around and read at the end of a normal exhale.

Let the arm hang relaxed at your side. Find the midpoint between the tip of the shoulder and the elbow. Wrap the tape around the bicep at that midpoint, perpendicular to the long axis of the arm. Keep the tape snug but not compressing.

Stand with weight evenly on both feet. Wrap the tape around the largest part of the upper thigh, just below the gluteal fold. Keep the tape parallel to the floor and snug, but not compressing the muscle.
